claim: Sleep disruption is widespread in the modern age and contributes significantly to a wide array of negative health consequences in humans.
source: Sleep disruption is widespread in the modern age and contributes significantly to a wide array of negative health consequences in humans (Colten and Altevogt, 2006; Medic et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Sleep-like states likely evolved at least 740 million years ago.
source: Sleep is ubiquitous in the animal kingdom and sleep-like states likely evolved at least 740 million years ago (Campbell and Tobler, 1984; Freiberg, 2020; Kanaya et al., 2020; Keene and Duboue, 2018; Nath et al., 2017; Webb, 1974).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Drosophila melanogaster has proved to be a useful model organism for understanding the molecular and cellular mechanisms regulating sleep.
source: The vinegar fly Drosophila melanogaster has proved to be a useful model organism for understanding the molecular and cellular mechanisms regulating sleep (Hendricks et al., 2000; Shaw et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Male flies display variable levels of increased sleep following nighttime sleep deprivation of around 0–25 min, compared to 200–500 min of sleep lost.
source: For example, male flies display variable levels of increased sleep following nighttime sleep deprivation of around 0–25 min, compared to 200–500 min of sleep lost (in 6 and 12 hr deprivation windows) and this is usually detectable only during the first few hours of the day after deprivation has ended (Geissmann et al., 2019; Geissmann et al., 2017; Hendricks et al., 2000; Huber et al., 2004; Klose and Shaw, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: 800 min of sleep loss in a full diurnal cycle was followed by only 100 min of recovery sleep (~12.5%) in Drosophila.
source: Furthermore, homeostatic sleep rebound in Drosophila appears to repay a relatively small proportion of the sleep lost during deprivation; 800 min of sleep loss in a full diurnal cycle was followed by only 100 min of recovery sleep (~12.5%) (Huber et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Humans can reclaim around 40% of the sleep lost to deprivation.
source: For example, humans can reclaim around 40% of the sleep lost to deprivation (Stroemel-Scheder and Lautenbacher, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Mechanical shaking is known to produce the biochemical hallmarks of stress, even when delivered during times of wakefulness.
source: Indeed, mechanical shaking is known to produce the biochemical hallmarks of stress, even when delivered during times of wakefulness (Harbison and Sehgal, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: In mammals, sleep consists of multiple, physiologically discrete stages, which differentially respond to sleep deprivation.
source: In mammals, sleep consists of multiple, physiologically discrete stages, which differentially respond to sleep deprivation (Achermann et al., 1993; Berger and Oswald, 1962; Endo et al., 1997; Everson et al., 1989; Loomis et al., 1937; Rechtschaffen et al., 1999; Takahashi et al., 1978).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Slow-wave sleep is preferentially increased following sleep deprivation when compared to rapid eye movement (REM) sleep.
source: Slow-wave sleep is also preferentially increased following sleep deprivation when compared to rapid eye movement (REM) sleep (Berger and Oswald, 1962; Borbly and Neuhaus, 1979; Dijk et al., 1990; Williams et al., 1964).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: A deep sleep state in flies is characterized by distinct patterns of brain signaling.
source: A growing body of evidence indicates the existence of a deep sleep state in flies, which is characterized by distinct patterns of brain signaling (Nitz et al., 2002; van Alphen et al., 2013), reduced metabolic rate (Stahl et al., 2017), and waste clearance from the brain (van Alphen et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: A deep sleep state in flies is characterized by reduced metabolic rate.
source: A growing body of evidence indicates the existence of a deep sleep state in flies, which is characterized by distinct patterns of brain signaling (Nitz et al., 2002; van Alphen et al., 2013), reduced metabolic rate (Stahl et al., 2017), and waste clearance from the brain (van Alphen et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: A deep sleep state in flies is characterized by waste clearance from the brain.
source: A growing body of evidence indicates the existence of a deep sleep state in flies, which is characterized by distinct patterns of brain signaling (Nitz et al., 2002; van Alphen et al., 2013), reduced metabolic rate (Stahl et al., 2017), and waste clearance from the brain (van Alphen et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Flies deprived of sleep for 6, 12, and 24 hr using 2 s of mechanical stimulation delivered at random times within each 20 s interval displayed immediate increases in total sleep compared to undisturbed flies.
source: As previously described in multiple studies by others using the Drosophila Activity Monitor (DAM) system, flies deprived of sleep for 6, 12, and 24 hr using 2 s of mechanical stimulation delivered at random times within each 20 s interval displayed immediate increases in total sleep compared to undisturbed flies (Figure 1A, D and G; Cirelli et al., 2005; Hendricks et al., 2000; Huber et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures and citations to published literature

claim: Flies deprived of sleep using 20 s trigger frequencies displayed significant 24 hr rebound when compared to undisturbed flies.
source: In each of these instances a significant 24 hr rebound was observed when compared to undisturbed flies (Figure 1C, F, I).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures

claim: Lowering the mechanical stimulation frequency to once every 220 s produced sleep deprivation for all the deprivation durations tested.
source: In order to examine the effects of stimulation frequency on sleep rebound, we decreased the mechanical stimulation frequency to once every 220 s. This low-frequency trigger produced sleep deprivation for all the deprivation durations tested (Figure 1B, E, and H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures

claim: No sleep rebound was observed for 6 hr, 12 hr, or 24 hr deprivation experiments using 220 s trigger frequencies, despite the fact that the lower frequency stimulations effectively deprived sleep.
source: Surprisingly, no sleep rebound was observed for 6 hr, 12 hr, or 24 hr deprivation experiments, despite the fact that the lower frequency stimulations effectively deprived sleep (Figure 1C, F, I).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures

claim: The 6 hr deprivation protocol produced higher sleep rebound than did 12 hr and 24 hr deprivation, despite the fact that this duration produced the smallest loss of sleep.
source: Examination of the magnitudes of sleep rebound following high-frequency mechanical deprivation revealed that the 6 hr deprivation protocol produced higher sleep rebound than did 12 hr and 24 hr deprivation, despite the fact that this duration produced the smallest loss of sleep (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figure

claim: Significant rebound was found only for the flies deprived with 20 s trigger frequencies when comparing 24 hr of sleep deprivation with stimulation frequencies of 20 s, 120 s, and 220 s.
source: Remarkably, we found significant rebound only for the flies deprived with 20 s trigger frequencies (Figure 1K).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figure

claim: The Ethoscope allows the user to deliver mechanical stimuli to individual flies only when a fly is inactive for a specified amount of time.
source: In contrast to the DAM system, which requires the simultaneous mechanical perturbation of all flies within the same DAM, the Ethoscope allows the user to deliver mechanical stimuli to individual flies only when a fly is inactive for a specified amount of time (Geissmann et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Canton-S flies failed to display significant increases in sleep during the 24 hr following deprivation when compared to undisturbed flies using 220 s inactivity triggers in Ethoscopes.
source: For both Canton-S and w1118, when compared to undisturbed flies, the sleep-deprived flies failed to display significant increases in sleep during the 24 hr following deprivation (Figure 2B and D); a surprising result given the clear effectiveness of sleep deprivation (Figure 2A and C), but consistent with the lack of rebound in similar situations using the vortexer (see Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures

claim: w1118 flies failed to display significant increases in sleep during the 24 hr following deprivation when compared to undisturbed flies using 220 s inactivity triggers in Ethoscopes.
source: For both Canton-S and w1118, when compared to undisturbed flies, the sleep-deprived flies failed to display significant increases in sleep during the 24 hr following deprivation (Figure 2B and D); a surprising result given the clear effectiveness of sleep deprivation (Figure 2A and C), but consistent with the lack of rebound in similar situations using the vortexer (see Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures

claim: Yoked controls suffered only partial sleep loss compared to focal flies.
source: Indeed, using the 220 s inactivity trigger allowed yoked flies to attain sleep while the focal fly was active (Figure 2F and G). Yoked controls, therefore, suffered only partial sleep loss compared to focal flies (Figure 2H and J).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures

claim: A comparison of total sleep across the entire 24 hr of the post-deprivation day revealed significantly higher levels of sleep in the focal flies compared to yoked controls for both Canton-S and w1118.
source: A comparison of total sleep across the entire 24 hr of the post-deprivation day revealed significantly higher levels of sleep in the focal flies compared to yoked controls for both Canton-S and w1118 (Figure 2I and K).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures

claim: Mechanical stimulation during deprivation significantly increased the activity levels of sleep-deprived flies a day after mechanical perturbation, when compared to undisturbed controls.
source: Indeed, we found that mechanical stimulation during deprivation significantly increased the activity levels of sleep-deprived flies a day after mechanical perturbation, when compared to undisturbed controls. This increase was seen immediately after the light-to-dark transition, that is, at the time associated with the transition to nighttime sleep (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), and most likely masked the 24 hr sleep rebound when compared to undisturbed flies.
evidence: Supported by data shown in figure supplement

claim: When compared to paired yoked controls, focal animals showed significant increases in cumulative sleep across two cycles.
source: When compared to yoked controls, focal sleep-deprived flies displayed modest but significant increases in cumulative sleep over two successive cycles (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figure

claim: Focal flies failed to discharge a substantial portion of the sleep debt accrued during deprivation.
source: Despite this apparent two-cycle rebound, focal flies failed to discharge a substantial portion of the sleep debt accrued during deprivation (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figure

claim: There was a significant increase in bout duration in the focal flies compared to yoked controls across the first 2 days following deprivation.
source: Though the number of sleep bouts was not significantly different between focal and yoked flies across any of the three post-deprivation cycles (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), there was a significant increase in bout duration in the focal flies compared to yoked controls across the first 2 days following deprivation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figure supplement

claim: Inactivity criteria of 25 min or more resulted in the largest payback of lost sleep when examined on the third day of recovery from deprivation.
source: We found that inactivity criteria of 25 min or more resulted in the largest payback of lost sleep when examined on the third day of recovery from deprivation (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figure

claim: When an inactivity criterion of 25 min was employed, sleep recovery approached ~50% of lost sleep by the third day of recovery.
source: When we employed an inactivity criterion of 25 min, a duration that likely reflects a relatively deep sleep state (Stahl et al., 2017) sleep recovery approached ~50% of lost sleep by the third day of recovery, a much higher proportion than was apparent using the currently employed unitary definition of sleep as bouts of inactivity lasting 5 min or more.
evidence: Supported by data analysis and citation to published literature

claim: At least half of all sleep-deprived flies paid back more than 50% of the sleep they lost during the 24 hr of deprivation when using a 25 min inactivity criterion.
source: At least half of all sleep-deprived flies paid back more than 50% of the sleep they lost during the 24 hr of deprivation, and over 25% of flies overshot their sleep debt, thereby displaying a defining hallmark of homeostatic control (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figure

claim: Over 25% of flies overshot their sleep debt when using a 25 min inactivity criterion.
source: At least half of all sleep-deprived flies paid back more than 50% of the sleep they lost during the 24 hr of deprivation, and over 25% of flies overshot their sleep debt, thereby displaying a defining hallmark of homeostatic control (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figure

claim: All unperturbed control flies routinely displayed 25 min or longer bouts of inactivity.
source: Indeed, all unperturbed control flies routinely displayed 25 min or longer bouts of inactivity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figure supplement

claim: Focal flies displayed significant increases in total long-bout sleep when compared to yoked controls on days 2 and 3 of recovery.
source: When total long-bout sleep across three successive cycles was quantified, focal flies displayed significant increases in such sleep when compared only to yoked controls on days 2 and 3 of recovery (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures

claim: Setting the Ethoscope's inactivity-dependent trigger to rotate tubes only when focal flies had been immobile for 22 min prevented flies from attaining 25 min of uninterrupted inactivity.
source: To test this prediction, we set the Ethoscope's inactivity-dependent trigger to rotate tubes only when focal flies had been immobile for 22 min as a means to prevent flies from attaining 25 min of uninterrupted inactivity.
evidence: Supported by experimental design description

claim: When using the standard inactivity duration criterion for sleep (5 min or more), 22 min trigger latency supported what appeared to be largely normal sleep rhythms in both focal and yoked flies.
source: When using the standard inactivity duration criterion for sleep (5 min or more), this long trigger latency supported what appeared to be largely normal sleep rhythms in both focal and yoked flies (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figure

claim: 22 min triggers effectively deprived flies of long-duration sleep while permitting yoked flies to achieve appreciable amounts of such sleep during focal deprivation.
source: Employing a 25 min inactivity duration criterion to remove short-bout sleep from our analysis revealed that 22 min triggers effectively deprived flies of long-duration sleep while permitting yoked flies to achieve appreciable amounts of such sleep during focal deprivation (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figure

claim: When behavior was analyzed using the standard 5 min inactivity criterion, focal flies displayed no significant increases in total sleep when compared to yoked controls following 22 min trigger deprivation.
source: When behavior was analyzed using the standard 5 min inactivity criterion, which would include short-bout sleep, focal flies displayed no significant increases in total sleep when compared to yoked controls (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figure

claim: When short-bout sleep was eliminated from the analysis through the use of a 25 min inactivity criterion, focal flies displayed significantly higher levels of long-bout sleep across all 3 days following deprivation.
source: In contrast, when short-bout sleep was eliminated from the analysis through the use of a 25 min inactivity criterion, focal flies displayed significantly higher levels of long-bout sleep across all 3 days following deprivation (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figure

claim: Focal flies were characterized by an increased number of bouts that were longer than 25 min compared to yoked controls following long-bout-specific deprivation.
source: Long-bout-specific deprivation also produced significant effects on sleep architecture. Focal flies were characterized by an increased number of bouts that were longer than 25 min compared to yoked controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), although the durations of these longer sleep bouts did not increase (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figure supplement

claim: When comparing sleep-deprived flies to unperturbed controls, 127 peaks displayed statistically significantly higher amplitudes in sections from focal flies.
source: When we compared the heights of these peaks between focal, sleep-deprived flies and unperturbed controls, we found 127 peaks that displayed statistically significantly higher amplitudes in sections from focal flies compared to those of unperturbed flies (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figure

claim: When yoked controls are included in the analysis, approximately half of the discernable m/z value peaks displayed statistically indistinguishable levels in the central brain across the undisturbed, yoked, and focal samples.
source: When yoked controls are included in the analysis, approximately half of the discernable m/z value peaks displayed statistically indistinguishable levels in the central brain across the undisturbed, yoked, and focal samples (Figure 6E, 'NS', 45%).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figure

claim: Seventy-three of the m/z peaks displayed the relative abundances expected of molecules tracking mechanical perturbation.
source: Seventy-three of the m/z peaks displayed the relative abundances expected of molecules tracking mechanical perturbation (38.8%), whereas only eight displayed the relative abundances expected of molecules tracking sleep pressure (~4%, Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figure

claim: Only eight m/z peaks displayed the relative abundances expected of molecules tracking sleep pressure.
source: Seventy-three of the m/z peaks displayed the relative abundances expected of molecules tracking mechanical perturbation (38.8%), whereas only eight displayed the relative abundances expected of molecules tracking sleep pressure (~4%, Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figure

claim: Two of the eight molecules identified in the first screen as tracking sleep pressure displayed the relative abundances expected of a sleep pressure tracking molecule in a replicate experiment.
source: Despite the markedly lower sensitivity of this replicate, we found that two of the eight molecules identified in the first screen as tracking sleep pressure, once again displayed the relative abundances expected of a sleep pressure tracking molecule.
evidence: Supported by replicate experimental data

claim: The 177.1 m/z peak corresponds to serotonin.
source: The 177.1 m/z peak has previously been shown to correspond to serotonin (Cao et al., 2019; Moriarty et al., 2011) and fits the molecular weight range of serotonin (176.2) in a positive ion matrix like DHB, which adds a cation with a single positive charge to the m/z peak, which for serotonin would result in a peak at ~177 m/z.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature and knowledge of mass spectrometry

claim: Serotonin is a strong candidate for a molecule whose abundance reflects sleep pressure in the fly's central brain.
source: Thus, serotonin would appear to be a strong candidate for a molecule whose abundance reflects sleep pressure in the fly's central brain (see Discussion), that follows the expected pattern across unperturbed, yoked, and focal flies (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figure and inference from experimental results

claim: Pharmacological increases in serotonin and the excitation of serotonergic neurons produce increases in baseline sleep in the fly.
source: Pharmacological increases in serotonin and the excitation of serotonergic neurons produce increases in baseline sleep in the fly (Haynes et al., 2015; Pooryasin and Fiala, 2015; Yuan et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Blocking synaptic transmission in single pairs of serotonergic neurons have been reported to reduce baseline sleep.
source: Similarly, blocking synaptic transmission in single pairs of serotonergic neurons have been reported to reduce baseline sleep (Alekseyenko et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Genetic loss of serotonin synthesis decreases baseline sleep.
source: Genetic loss of serotonin synthesis decreases baseline sleep, as does the loss of 5HT-R-1A and 5HT-R-2B serotonin receptors (Qian et al., 2017; Yuan et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Loss of serotonin and the serotonin receptor 5HT-R-2B results in a reduction in sleep rebound following deprivation.
source: Loss of serotonin and the serotonin receptor 5HT-R-2B also results in a reduction in sleep rebound following deprivation (Qian et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Loss of the serotonin transporter dSERT is associated with significant increases in sleep.
source: Finally, loss of the serotonin transporter dSERT, which normally functions to remove extracellular serotonin, is associated with significant increases in sleep (Knapp et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Genetic loss of arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase is accompanied by both increased homeostatic sleep rebound and brain serotonin levels following sleep deprivation.
source: Furthermore, the genetic loss of arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase, which normally functions to inactivate serotonin and dopamine, is accompanied by both increased homeostatic sleep rebound and brain serotonin levels following sleep deprivation, consistent with serotonin acting as a sleep substance during mechanical deprivation (Davla et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Deep sleep states are the primary target of homeostatic control in Drosophila.
source: Our results reveal that deep sleep states are the primary target of homeostatic control and establish the presence of multi-cycle sleep rebound following deprivation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Multi-cycle sleep rebound follows deprivation in Drosophila.
source: Our results reveal that deep sleep states are the primary target of homeostatic control and establish the presence of multi-cycle sleep rebound following deprivation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Specific deprivation of deep sleep states results in state-specific homeostatic rebound.
source: Furthermore, we establish that specific deprivation of deep sleep states results in state-specific homeostatic rebound.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Serotonin levels track sleep pressure in the fly's central brain.
source: Finally, by accounting for the molecular effects of mechanical stimulation during deprivation experiments, we show that serotonin levels track sleep pressure in the fly's central brain.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Longer bouts of sleep are a better reflection of sleep homeostasis than traditional definitions of sleep in the fly.
source: Furthermore, our recent analyses suggest that longer bouts of sleep are a better reflection of sleep homeostasis than traditional definitions of sleep in the fly (Abhilash and Shafer, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Flies display two daily peaks of long-bout sleep, with approximately twice as much deep sleep taking place at night.
source: Unperturbed controls displayed two daily peaks of long-bout sleep, with approximately twice as much deep sleep taking place at night, as previously described (Hendricks et al., 2000; Stahl et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Flies display both longer and deeper bouts of sleep at night.
source: Flies display both longer and deeper bouts of sleep at night (Hendricks et al., 2000; van Alphen et al., 2013) and deeper sleep is associated with distinct patterns of global brain activity when compared to brain activity during wakefulness or during more brief and shallow bouts sleep (Nitz et al., 2002; Tainton-Heap et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Longer sleep bouts are attended by lower metabolic rates, where bout lengths of 60 min were shown to be associated with the lowest rates.
source: Longer sleep bouts are also attended by lower metabolic rates, where bout lengths of 60 min were shown to be associated with the lowest rates (Stahl et al., 2017), a phenomenon similar to that observed for deeper NREM sleep stages in humans (Berger and Phillips, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Flies display a stereotyped pattern of proboscis movements that appear to drive waste clearance.
source: Finally, flies display a stereotyped pattern of proboscis movements that appear to drive waste clearance (van Alphen et al., 2021), reminiscent of the changes in fluid dynamics observed in the cerebrospinal fluid of sleeping mammals, that occur at times corresponding to deep sleep stages (Fultz et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Bouts of inactivity longer than anything between 30 and 60 min are stronger reflections of the daily homeostatic control sleep than shorter bouts of sleep.
source: Finally, recent work from our lab has suggested that bouts of inactivity longer than anything between 30 and 60 min are stronger reflections of the daily homeostatic control sleep than shorter bouts of sleep (Abhilash and Shafer, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Mechanical shaking only during times of wakefulness increased molecular signatures of stress, even when given for relatively short periods.
source: However, mechanical shaking only during times of wakefulness increased molecular signatures of stress, even when given for relatively short periods (Harbison and Sehgal, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Previous work using the Ethoscope system has revealed remarkably low levels of homeostatic rebound and no sleep deprivation-associated death.
source: Previous work using this system has revealed remarkably low levels of homeostatic rebound and no sleep deprivation-associated death (Geissmann et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Gentle handling of rodent subjects has significant effects on feeding behavior following deprivation.
source: Chronic mechanical agitation also produces stress (Meerlo et al., 2008; Sgoifo et al., 2006; Tartar et al., 2009), and even gentle handling of rodent subjects, a means of deprivation thought to cause little stress, has significant effects on feeding behavior following deprivation (Dukanovic et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Chronic mechanical agitation produces stress.
source: Chronic mechanical agitation also produces stress (Meerlo et al., 2008; Sgoifo et al., 2006; Tartar et al., 2009), and even gentle handling of rodent subjects, a means of deprivation thought to cause little stress, has significant effects on feeding behavior following deprivation (Dukanovic et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: A previous study using HPLC to examine serotonin levels in dissected brains failed to observe serotonin increases in sleep-deprived flies.
source: A previous study using HPLC to examine serotonin levels in dissected brains failed to observe serotonin increases in sleep-deprived flies (Davla et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Sleep loss-driven serotonin increases take place in the central brain and not the optic lobes.
source: However, the spatial resolution provided by MALDI-TOF imaging suggests that sleep loss-driven serotonin increases take place in the central brain and not the optic lobes (e.g., Figure 6B and F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures

claim: Serotonin does not build up throughout the optic lobes.
source: We therefore suspect that serotonin does not build up throughout the optic lobes and that whole-brain assays might therefore fail to detect the sleep loss-induced changes we describe here.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations and reasoning

claim: Whole-brain assays might fail to detect sleep loss-induced changes in serotonin.
source: We therefore suspect that serotonin does not build up throughout the optic lobes and that whole-brain assays might therefore fail to detect the sleep loss-induced changes we describe here.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations and reasoning
